quote: $y$ sei eindeutige[?] algebraische Funktion [-...-] von $x$, so dass $f(y,x)=0$ wo $f$ ganzzahlige Coefficienten habe. $y$ sei rational für alle rationalen Werte von [-...-] [-...-] $x$ für $\alpha \leqq x \leqq \beta$
english: Let y be a single-valued algebraic function of x such that f(y,x)=0, where f has integer coefficients. Let y be rational for all rational values of x with α ≤ x ≤ β.
topic: Notes on when the intersection of two forms F=0 and f=0 is irreducible (expressing lmF = Aφ + Bf), a problem of passing an ellipse of given shape through three given points, and a study of an algebraic function y of x that takes rational values for all rational x in an interval, using a linear fractional substitution.

triage.modern_statement: Suppose y = y(x) is a single-valued (real-analytic) branch of an algebraic function on an interval [α,β], meaning F(x,y(x)) = 0 for some F ∈ Z[x,y]. If y(x) is rational for every rational x in [α,β], must y be a rational function of x, i.e. y ∈ Q(x)? Put another way: an algebraic function that is not rational cannot take rational values at all rational points of a real interval. This is the key analytic lemma behind Hilbert's irreducibility theorem. The note's linear fractional substitution x = (a t + b)/(c t + d) maps the interval onto a neighbourhood of t = ∞. Hilbert's proof then works with series expansions there.
triage.answered_by: David Hilbert himself, in 'Ueber die Irreducibilität ganzer rationaler Functionen mit ganzzahligen Coefficienten', J. reine angew. Math. 110 (1892), 104–129. The result became the core of Hilbert's irreducibility theorem. Later refinements include M. Fried, 'On Hilbert's irreducibility theorem', J. Number Theory 6 (1974), and modern expositions such as arXiv:1809.10977.

evidence.claim: Hilbert published 'Ueber die Irreducibilität ganzer rationaler Functionen mit ganzzahligen Coefficienten' in J. reine angew. Math. 110 (1892), pp. 104–129.

Hilbert's irreducibility theorem, conceived by Hilbert in 1892, says that irreducible polynomials over Q(X1..Xr) stay irreducible after substituting suitable rational values (in fact infinitely many).

Modern expositions of Hilbert's proof follow the same steps as the note: assume a root function y is not a quotient of polynomials with rational coefficients, then choose rational s in an interval where the root values y_i(s) are not rational, which gives irreducibility of f(s,Y).
Fried (1974) revisits Hilbert's irreducibility theorem. Part of the argument concludes that x is a rational function when the function field is rational.

triage.why: The note asks whether an algebraic function with integer-coefficient defining equation must be rational if it is rational at all rational points of an interval. That is exactly the analytic heart of Hilbert's 1892 irreducibility paper: if y were not rational, it would have to take non-rational values at some rational points of any interval. The linear fractional substitution matches how the interval is moved to infinity for series expansions. The fragment's link to the 1892 paper is my own inference from matching content; no source quotes this diary page directly. The specific claim was settled by Hilbert's 1892 paper. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. Hilbert irreducibility and Hilbertian fields are still active research topics, for example the 2026 arXiv preprint by Kadets and Neftin on Hilbert irreducibility for algebraic points (arXiv:2606.10584), which turned up in my search.
